title: Arnett v. Kennedy
lead: A federal employee accused of reckless public accusations demands an impartial trial before discharge; the Supreme Court sustains the removal scheme through sharply different constitutional theories.

actors.name: Wayne Kennedy
actors.role: Nonprobationary competitive-service field representative in OEO’s Chicago Regional Office.

actors.name: Wendell Verduin
actors.role: Regional director whom Kennedy allegedly accused of misconduct and who initiated and decided the removal charges.

actors.name: Office of Economic Opportunity and Civil Service Commission
actors.role: Supplied administrative appeal routes with full evidentiary procedures after removal.

proceedings: Kennedy sued on the effective date of removal, March 27, 1972.
A three-judge district court granted Kennedy summary judgment, reinstatement and backpay, and a facial speech injunction.
On direct appeal, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded on April 16, 1974.
limits: The alleged bribery and Kennedy’s supposed recklessness remained disputed. The government’s material factual version was assumed to test Kennedy’s summary judgment. Five Justices sustained the procedures, six rejected the facial speech challenge, and only three adopted the statutory-benefit-and-procedure inseparability theory. This is the historical 1974 decision, separate from Loudermill.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A workplace accusation leads to proposed removal
sections.cue: Who accused whom, and which facts remained disputed?
paragraphs: Wayne Kennedy was a nonprobationary competitive-service field representative in the Chicago Regional Office of the Office of Economic Opportunity. On February 18, 1972, Regional Director Wendell Verduin sent Kennedy a proposed adverse-action notice charging misconduct in five incidents from November and December 1971.

The central charge concerned Kennedy’s alleged public accusation that Verduin and an assistant offered a community-action representative a $100,000 OEO grant in exchange for a statement against Kennedy and another employee. The notice asserted that Kennedy lacked proof, recklessly disregarded available facts, and damaged the officials’ authority and the office’s functioning. The alleged offer, its characterization as a bribe, and Kennedy’s supposed recklessness were contested; the Supreme Court did not determine that Kennedy fabricated the allegation.

The notice attached supporting material and advised Kennedy that he could inspect it, respond orally and in writing, and submit affidavits. His lawyer demanded an impartial trial-type hearing with confrontation, witnesses, a record, and findings, and asserted protected speech. The lawyer called the reported conversations inaccurate without offering a different factual account. Kennedy did not personally appear to contest the charges.

On March 20, Verduin sustained the charges and announced removal effective March 27. He advised Kennedy of appeal rights to OEO or the Civil Service Commission. The initial deciding official was thus also a target of the alleged accusation, a fact that later divided the Justices independently of the facial validity of the procedures.

sources.pinpoint: 416 U.S. at 137–140, 175–176, 196–197 & cited notes; Facts and competing accounts

sections.title: The statutory scheme offers reply before removal and a trial-type appeal afterward
sections.cue: What protections came from statute and regulations together?
paragraphs: The Lloyd-La Follette Act, then 5 U.S.C. § 7501, allowed removal or unpaid suspension only for cause promoting service efficiency. It required written charges and reasons, reasonable time for a written answer and affidavits, and an early written decision. A hearing or examination of witnesses before removal remained within the removing official’s discretion.

Regulations supplied at least thirty days’ advance notice, detailed reasons, access to evidence, an oral as well as written response, identification of sustained charges, and appeal rights. The oral reply was an opportunity to persuade, not an adversary trial. On appeal through OEO or the Commission, however, a full evidentiary hearing included sworn testimony and cross-examination. Rules governed participation, witnesses, accepted documents, transcripts or agreed summaries, and protection against interference with witnesses.

The appeal routes did not run concurrently. A direct Commission appeal waived agency appeal; an agency appeal could be followed by Commission review. OEO ordinarily held the trial-type hearing after removal. Reinstatement carried backpay less interim earnings. These protections derived from the combined statutory and regulatory scheme, including the Veterans’ Preference Act and executive extension of its protections, rather than from the original Lloyd-La Follette text alone.

sources.pinpoint: 416 U.S. at 140–148 & nn.5–16; Litigation and governing procedures

sections.title: Kennedy obtains reinstatement without a trial on the disputed accusations
sections.cue: What exactly did the district court decide?
paragraphs: Kennedy sued on March 27, 1972, seeking declaratory and injunctive relief for the absence of a full pre-removal hearing and alleged speech retaliation. A single district judge referred the procedural constitutional issue to a three-judge court and dismissed the individual speech claim pending administrative exhaustion. Kennedy amended to raise facial vagueness and overbreadth, adding eighteen largely nominal plaintiffs. Class certification was deferred.

The three-judge court granted Kennedy summary judgment, ordered reinstatement and backpay, required constitutionally sufficient proceedings before future removal, and enjoined enforcement of the Act and rules as regulations of competitive employees’ speech. His Commission appeal had been delayed by litigation and ended after court-ordered reinstatement.

The government appealed directly to the Supreme Court. Because Kennedy had obtained summary judgment despite conflicting affidavits, Justice Rehnquist treated the government’s material account as true for deciding the legal issues. The question was whether the scheme remained unconstitutional even on that account, not whether the government had proved the accusations at a merits hearing.

sections.title: Rehnquist treats the employment benefit and its procedures as inseparable
sections.cue: Why was this influential theory only a plurality position?
paragraphs: Justice Rehnquist announced the judgment, joined by Chief Justice Burger and Justice Stewart. He traced civil-service security from patronage through the Pendleton Act, McKinley’s just-cause rule, and the 1912 legislation. Congress expanded tenure protection while deliberately avoiding a mandatory elaborate removal trial.

Applying Roth’s account of property created by independent law, Rehnquist recognized an expectancy of continued employment for cause but included the prescribed method of determining cause within that expectancy’s dimensions. Separating tenure from procedure would give an employee a right Congress withheld in the same enactment. He also invoked decisions disfavoring retention of statutory benefits while attacking vital conditions, acknowledging that principle’s uneven application. On this view, the benefit carried its limited enforcement mechanism and did not require an adversary hearing before discharge.

Rehnquist distinguished welfare termination, garnishment, replevin, and license cases by both the interests involved and the procedural limits he considered part of this employment interest. Separately, an unsupported dishonesty charge accompanying discharge could implicate liberty through reputational harm, but the relevant hearing served name clearing. A post-removal appeal could provide that opportunity despite delays exceeding three months in many cases.

His property analysis made a constitutional decision about Verduin’s personal involvement unnecessary. He also rejected Justice White’s proposed statutory neutrality requirement: supervisors commonly participated in disputes, and replacing a personally involved agency head could require an outside official inconsistent with Congress’s relatively simple process. Only three Justices accepted this benefit-and-procedure theory; six rejected it.

sections.title: Powell and Blackmun sustain the procedures through constitutional balancing
sections.cue: How could the result survive rejection of the plurality’s premise?
paragraphs: Justice Powell, joined by Justice Blackmun, agreed with the procedural result but rejected Rehnquist’s premise. For-cause tenure created a legitimate entitlement under Roth and Sindermann. Legislatures could choose whether to create that property interest, but could not then define away constitutionally necessary safeguards. Otherwise any statutory property could be taken without notice or hearing merely by attaching that limitation to the grant.

Powell instead balanced competing interests. Government needed efficient work, discipline, functioning offices, and prompt removal of disruptive employees. A prior trial could impose expense and delay and discourage justified discharge. Loss of pay seriously burdened the employee, but reinstatement and backpay were available, along with possible private resources, other employment, or welfare. Powell distinguished the immediate subsistence threat in Goldberg.

Thirty days’ notice, access to evidence, oral and written reply, affidavits, and a later full hearing sufficiently reduced initial error in his assessment. Paid suspension did not answer every governmental cost or deterrence concern. He also rejected a requirement of an impartial initial decisionmaker: a supervisor often knew the facts best, and educating a new official could turn screening into a preliminary trial. An impartial post-removal adjudicator sufficed. Powell applied the same balance to the liberty claim.

sources.pinpoint: 416 U.S. at 164–171 & nn.1–6; Powell and Blackmun

sections.title: White accepts preliminary screening but objects to Verduin deciding this case
sections.cue: What narrower ground would have preserved Kennedy’s relief?
paragraphs: Justice White agreed that property and constitutionally sufficient procedure were distinct. His historical analysis of property takings, licensing, attachments, public employment, and security adjudication distinguished preliminary deprivation from final adjudication. Risks such as destruction, dissipation, or danger could justify immediate action, but public origin of an interest did not eliminate the right to a hearing. For-cause employment differed from at-will employment, and older rights-versus-privileges reasoning had been undermined.

White considered the risk of error, temporary loss, appeal delays, the danger posed by advance notice, and uncompensated governmental or private costs. Studies showed substantial reversal rates and often lengthy personnel appeals. An employee could not abscond with a job, and paid suspension could protect operations, though it cost the government. White ultimately accepted advance notice and written presentation as preliminary probable-cause screening, with a full hearing and cross-examination on appeal. Goldberg’s especially severe deprivation justified greater initial process there.

Verduin’s direct personal stake was different. His own reputation was implicated, yet he assembled the charges and decided to discharge their author. White did not require recusal for routine supervisory disagreement. Through constitutional avoidance, he would read the statute’s silence to require a qualified impartial initial official in these circumstances. He would preserve reinstatement and backpay on that ground while reversing the facial speech injunction. The five Justices sustaining the procedural result rejected his proposed neutrality requirement.

sections.title: Six Justices reject the facial speech challenge
sections.cue: Why did that ruling leave the individual speech defense unresolved?
paragraphs: Rehnquist’s speech analysis gained the agreement of Powell, Blackmun, and White, producing six votes. The service-efficiency standard governed many occupations and supplied general employment protection rather than a criminal code. Congress need not choose between an exhaustive list of misconduct and no tenure protection. Employment principles, the personnel manual, and access to agency counsel supplied context.

Under Pickering, government as employer had interests concerning employee speech different from its power over citizens generally. The opinion construed cause to exclude constitutionally protected speech while reaching speech improperly impairing agency efficiency and reputation. On the government’s assumed account, satisfactorily proved reckless defamatory accusations could justify removal. The facial ruling did not adjudicate Kennedy’s individual claim that his actual speech was protected.

sources.pinpoint: 416 U.S. at 158–163 & nn.24–25; Facial speech challenge

sections.title: Douglas and Marshall dispute both the practical balance and the speech protection
sections.cue: What did the dissenters think the delayed hearing failed to protect?
paragraphs: Justice Douglas separately rejected sacrificing speech on public affairs because it offended supervisors or disrupted harmony. He warned that bureaucratic assessment could reward conformity rather than useful work, and discussed personal attacks and recusal, institutional compliance versus performance, and impermissible employment discrimination. He also joined Justice Marshall’s dissent, as did Justice Brennan.

Marshall would affirm both district-court grounds. Continued employment, retirement benefits, salary progression, and insurance were substantial property; discharge could stigmatize and impede other work. Disputed testimonial charges required confrontation, cross-examination, defense witnesses, and an independent decisionmaker before removal. He emphasized appeal reversal rates and delays, Kennedy’s debts and lost insurance, and Kennedy’s resort to public assistance despite a $16,000 salary. Backpay could not restore lost housing, education, or family stability; welfare was neither immediate nor guaranteed and could require exhaustion of assets.

Marshall also challenged the claimed administrative necessity. Nine agencies already offered pre-removal evidentiary hearings. An Administrative Conference study recommended them and suggested scheduling, rather than hearing length, caused much delay. Hearings could fit within the thirty-day notice period; leave or reassignment could contain disruption; one adequate early hearing might reduce later proceedings. Verduin’s combined roles demonstrated the inadequacy of informal reply.

On speech, Marshall thought the efficiency formula could chill truthful exposure of misconduct, partly the very conduct the legislation sought to protect. Declaring protected speech exempt gave insufficient guidance to employees beyond Kennedy. He proposed clearer distinctions involving official versus private speech, truth and reasonable belief, public concern, and confidential information.

On April 16, 1974, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded. Five Justices sustained the procedures and six rejected the facial speech challenge, but the three-vote inseparability theory did not become a majority rule. The assigned excerpt juxtaposing Rehnquist and Powell omits much of this division; the adjacent Loudermill reading concerns a separate later decision.
